title: The Harvest of Cold Spring
premise: Tamsin Whitlock, a hospice nurse in the decaying village of Cold Spring, has spent twenty years rationalizing the backwards counting she hears from the dying. When the church bell—melted down in 1911—rings again, Tamsin learns the founders bound something beneath the village with a ritual that must be renewed every generation, and the last keeper died without passing it on. The dying count backwards because they are being collected early to feed the debt. To save Cold Spring, Tamsin must complete the founders' ritual themselves—but doing so requires becoming the new keeper, sacrificing their invisibility, their name, and eventually their own voice to the bell.
about_author: Sebastian Nakamura is a former mortuary technician who writes horror rooted in small-town complicity and quiet dread. They live off-grid in the Pacific Northwest and refuse to be photographed.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At Hollow Pines hospice, Tamsin cares for Edith Marlowe, who counts down from one hundred in her sleep—and dies precisely at zero, hours before any prognosis said she would. Tamsin logs it as coincidence, the twentieth such log entry. Emotional beat: controlled denial beginning to crack; the reader sees how carefully Tamsin has built a life of not-noticing.

chapters.title: A Bell That Isn't There
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At dawn the church bell rings nine times, though parish records confirm it was melted for scrap in 1911. Only Tamsin and a mute boy, Wren Ashby, seem to hear it. In the empty belfry there is no bell—only a scorched circle of rope. Emotional beat: vertigo; the rational scaffolding of Tamsin's life collapses in a single morning.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with an intercut 1911 diary excerpt from founder Abigail Crane. Researching in the flooded archive cellar, Tamsin finds the Ledger: names crossed out in generations, each dated to a deathbed countdown. The final page lists Tamsin's own name, uncrossed, with today's date beside it. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: Everyone Knew
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin confronts the village council—Dr. Pell, shopkeeper Ruth Okafor, and Mayor Hensley—who admit the truth: Cold Spring's prosperity was purchased by the ritual, and every elder is complicit. They beg Tamsin to accept the keeping quietly, as others did. Emotional beat: betrayal; the horror isn't the bell, it's the neighbors.

chapters.title: Wren Hears Everything
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The mute boy who hears the bell reveals, through drawings, that the thing below Cold Spring collects voices—it took his speech at age four when his mother tried to flee. He shows Tamsin where the founders' ritual circle lies: beneath the reservoir, which the council drained last month. Emotional beat: fragile alliance; loyalty forming between two people the village discarded.

chapters.title: What the Dying Know
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A dying patient, old Silas Crane (Abigail's descendant), gives Tamsin the missing rite: the debt can be closed, but only if someone volunteers freely before the count reaches zero—he whispers 'seven' and dies. The council, panicking, decides to force Wren instead. Emotional beat: grief braided with resolve; Tamsin stops being a bystander.

chapters.title: The Empty Reservoir
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Descending into the drained basin at night, Tamsin finds the ritual ring and the thing itself—a vast, patient absence that wears the voices of everyone Cold Spring has fed it, including Edith's. It offers Tamsin a bargain: walk away, and it will take only the guilty. Emotional beat: temptation; power offered to the powerless.

chapters.title: Nine Rings for Nine Names
chapters.summary: Alternating Tamsin and Wren POVs. The council drags Wren to the belfry to bind him as keeper. Tamsin races through a village gone wrong—streets looping, houses showing 1911 interiors—as the bell tolls each council member's name. Emotional beat: terror and fury; loyalty tested against self-preservation.

chapters.title: The Rite of Cold Spring
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At the belfry, Tamsin interrupts the binding, speaks Silas's rite aloud, and offers themselves freely—not to renew the debt but to close it, taking every voice the thing holds into their own throat. The bell materializes, rings once, and shatters. The council members who enabled a century of feeding are left nameless and hollow. Emotional beat: sacrificial climax; justice outside any law.

chapters.title: The Quiet After
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, months later. Cold Spring is ordinary now, its elders diminished, its dead resting uncounted. Wren speaks his first word in years—'Tamsin'—at a plain grave marker. On windless nights, he sometimes hears a single soft chime, and answers aloud. Emotional beat: mourning transmuted into vigil; the cost of truth paid in full, and honored.
